turns.t: Hi, doc. Sorry, I know I'm early. My sister dropped me off and she drives like there's a fire behind her.
No problem at all. Take a seat. What's been going on?
The nights have been really hard. I can't even tell you. Last night I sat on the porch till four a.m.
That sounds exhausting. So the nights have been really hard, and it's wearing you down.
Yes! And my neighbor's dog barking doesn't help, he's got this bark like a rusty gate.
Let's focus on you for a moment. Are you still taking your usual medicines?
Oh, yes. I take the olanzapine, 10 milligrams, at bedtime, same as always.
Olanzapine, 10 milligrams at bedtime. Got it. Anything else?
The sertraline, 50 mg every morning with my coffee.
Sertraline, 50 mg every morning. Nurse, could you check the chart for me?
Sure, one second. The chart here says olanzapine, 15 milligrams at bedtime.
Fifteen? No, no. It's 10. Isn't it? The pharmacy gave me those little white ones.
The last prescription on file does say 15, but I can't see the bottle.
So we have 10 from you and 15 on the chart. We'll sort that out, don't worry. Did you bring the bottle?
I left it at my sister's. She told me to bring it, and of course I forgot.
Easy fix, we'll call the pharmacy afterwards. And the sertraline matches the chart, nurse?
Yes, 50 mg in the morning matches.
Good. Have you had a diagnosis of anything in the past, anything long term?
Schizophrenia. Since my twenties. I've been pretty stable for years until this month.
Thank you for telling me. Any allergies to medicines that I should know about?
Allergies? No, none that I know of.
Okay, none known. Let me check your vitals. Your blood pressure is 126 over 78 and your pulse is 88.
Is that okay? I never know what the numbers are supposed to be.
Both numbers are fine for you right now. Hold your hands out in front of you for me.
Like this?
Yes. Your hands are steady. That's reassuring.
My sister always checks my hands, and I always worry about it. Silly, I know.
Plenty of people worry about that, and nothing here suggests it. Now, when did the nights get worse?
About the time my work changed shifts. I'm on the late schedule now, and it's a mess.
So a new shift, less sleep, and the nights getting harder. Is that fair?
That's fair. I get home at midnight, and then the evening just drags on and on.
Here's my impression. This is most likely stress and broken sleep from the shift change, making your nights tougher.
So it's not the medicine failing?
I can't tell yet, and that's why the dose question matters. I'd like to order a blood test to check your medicine levels.
Okay. Does it hurt?
Just a quick needle in the arm. The nurse will take you through to the lab after we're done.
Right this way when you're ready.
My sister's going to say I told you so about the bottle.
Ha. Tell her the pharmacy call is on me. And keep taking both medicines exactly as you do now until we know the dose.
Same as now. 10 at night, 50 in the morning, as I said.
As you remember them, yes. Until we confirm. Try to wind down an hour before bed, dim lights, no phone.
I can try. The phone is my worst habit.
Come back and see me in two weeks, and we'll go through the blood results together.
Two weeks. I'll put it in my calendar.
And if the nights get frightening before then, call the clinic, day or night.
I will. Thanks for not rushing me, doc.
Anytime. So, to recap: bloods today, pharmacy call, same medicines, and back in two weeks.
Got it. Bloods, pharmacy, same pills, two weeks.
Perfect. Take care of yourself.
Follow me, I'll walk you out.
Bye, everybody.
